snippet.title: The Madness That Made Sailors Walk Calmly Into the Sea
snippet.description: What calenture was, underneath all the bloodletting and the literary metaphor and the psychiatric papers, was something simpler and more unsettling than any of those framings quite captured. It was homesickness taken to its absolute limit. A man who had been at sea for months, weakened by heat and hunger and weeks of motionless equatorial sky, looked over the rail at water that had turned the colour of a summer field and felt the pull of everything he had left behind so intensely that his brain simply completed the picture for him, filled in the grass and the trees and sometimes the face of a sister gathering flowers, and then stepped back and let him walk toward it. The sea did not trick these men with violence or chaos. It offered them something beautiful, and they accepted.

He was the Quartermaster, the officer responsible for maintaining order, protecting the crew's interests, and ensuring that power was never concentrated in one person's hands. ⚔️📜

snippet.title: Edward Low: The Feared Pirate Who Crossed Every Line Imaginable
snippet.description:
Edward Low was born around 1690 in Westminster, which at the time was one of the roughest parts of London, a neighbourhood where poverty ran deep enough that crime was less a choice than a family trade. His household was built on it. Low's brother Richard made a name for himself as a child thief who pioneered a particular trick: he would have himself carried through a crowd in a basket, and from that vantage point he would snatch the expensive wigs off the heads of passing gentlemen, a scheme clever enough to get talked about and eventually written down. Richard was later hanged for burglary in 1707, and the fact that this barely slowed the rest of the family tells you what kind of environment produced Edward Low. He was cheating at cards before he was old enough to be taken seriously at a table, and by his teenage years he had graduated to pickpocketing and street theft with no sign that anything else was coming.
